title: The Twelve Sent Out
summary: Jesus gives his twelve disciples authority to heal and drive out spirits, names them, and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to announce that the kingdom of heaven is near. He tells them to travel light, to expect rejection, persecution, and division even within families, and not to fear, because their Father knows every sparrow. Whoever receives them receives him, and whoever receives him receives the One who sent him.
story:
At the end of chapter 9 Jesus saw the crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (9:36) and told his disciples to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out workers. Now he makes them the workers. The twelve, whom Matthew names here for the first time as a group, are sent to do what Jesus has been doing: Matthew twice summarized his ministry as teaching, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness (4:23, 9:35), and in verse 1 he gives the twelve authority to heal “every disease and sickness” in the same words.

This is the second of the five great discourses in Matthew, each closed by a formula (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). The first described life under God's reign; this one describes carrying its message into a world that will not always want it. The book introduction treats 8:1-11:1 as one unit: ten deeds of the Messiah in chapters 8 and 9, then the speech that sends his followers to extend them. Matthew never narrates the twelve setting out or coming back (contrast Mark 6:12-13, 30 and Luke 9:6, 10). The instructions begin with a mission limited to Israel and widen, from verse 16 on, into warnings about governors, kings, and Gentiles that reach past this first trip toward the church's later mission, so that Matthew's readers could hear the speech as addressed to them. Chapter 11 turns from the sending of the disciples to the reception of Jesus himself.
historical:
The mission is limited at first to Israel. Galilee was ringed by Gentile territory: the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon to the northwest, the Greek cities of the Decapolis to the southeast, and Samaria to the south. The Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel but held only the five books of Moses as Scripture and worshiped on Mount Gerizim; John Hyrcanus had destroyed their temple there around 110 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254-256), and hostility ran both ways. ‘The road of the Gentiles’ (verse 5) means travel into Gentile territory, not merely a highway.

The warnings of verses 17 and 18 fit the first century. ‘Councils’ (synedria) are the local Jewish courts that disciplined members of the community; the Mishnah later describes courts of twenty-three judges in the towns (m. Sanhedrin 1:6). Flogging was limited by Deuteronomy 25:2-3 to forty lashes, and the Mishnah stops at thirty-nine and assigns the task to the synagogue attendant (m. Makkot 3:10-12). Paul says he received thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Governors and kings held power over life and death. Pontius Pilate was prefect of Judea from about 26 to 36; Herod Agrippa I, ruling as king, beheaded James son of Zebedee, named in verse 2, around AD 44 (Acts 12:1-2); and Paul later stood before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa II (Acts 24 to 26). ‘Hated by everyone because of My name’ (verse 22) matches what Roman writers said of Christians. Tacitus describes Nero's punishment of Christians after the fire of Rome in 64, a group he calls hated for their vices (Annals 15.44), and Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia around 112, reports executing people for the name Christian alone (Letters 10.96).

The list of the twelve also appears in Mark 3:16-19, Luke 6:14-16, and Acts 1:13. The lists always begin with Simon Peter and, where he appears, end with Judas. Matthew arranges the names in pairs, perhaps reflecting the sending out two by two (Mark 6:7), calls Peter ‘first’, and alone calls Matthew ‘the tax collector’. Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark corresponds to ‘Judas son of James’ in Luke and Acts, most likely one man with two names. Simon is called ho Kananaios, from the Aramaic for zealous, which Luke renders ‘the Zealot’; it may mean zeal for the law or association with resistance to Rome, since the organized party of the Zealots is attested by Josephus only in the war of AD 66 to 70 (Jewish War 4.160-161). Iscariot is most often explained as ‘man of Kerioth’, a town in southern Judah (Joshua 15:25).

The coin of verse 29 is the assarion, a small Roman bronze coin worth one sixteenth of a denarius, a laborer's daily wage. Luke has five sparrows for two assaria (Luke 12:6), as if the fifth were thrown in free. Adolf Deissmann (Light from the Ancient East) drew attention to Diocletian's edict on maximum prices of AD 301, which lists sparrows by the ten and as the cheapest birds sold for food.
cultural:
Travelers carried coins in the folds of a belt or sash, a leather bag (pēra) for bread, a spare tunic for cold nights, sandals, and a staff for walking and for defense. The verb in verse 9 is ktaomai, ‘acquire’ or ‘procure’: the twelve are not to equip themselves for the road or earn their keep from their healing, since what they received freely they give freely (verse 8). Mark 6:8-9 allows a staff and sandals where Matthew and Luke 9:3 forbid a staff; harmonizers have suggested that Mark permits the staff one already has while Matthew forbids acquiring another, and others see the evangelists applying one tradition differently. The bag was the badge of the wandering Cynic philosophers, who begged; John Dominic Crossan (The Historical Jesus, 1991) pressed the comparison, but the twelve are to stay with one host rather than beg (verse 11). Josephus says the Essenes traveled carrying nothing but weapons against bandits, since members in every town supplied them (Jewish War 2.124-127). The saying ‘the worker is worthy of his provisions’ (verse 10) reappears in Paul's defense of support for ministers (1 Corinthians 9:14, 1 Timothy 5:18), and the Didache, a church manual from around AD 100, applies it to true prophets while warning that a traveling apostle who stays three days or asks for money is false (Didache 11.4-6, 13.1).

The greeting on entering a house was shalom, a blessing and not a pleasantry, which could ‘rest on’ a household or ‘return’ to the speaker. Shaking the dust off the feet was a public act of breaking off, treating a Jewish town that refused the message as foreign soil (compare Acts 13:51). Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19) were the Bible's byword for judgment.

The pairing of snakes and doves drew on familiar images. The serpent of Genesis 3:1 is ‘crafty’, and the Greek translation there uses phronimos, the word Jesus uses for shrewd; the dove could stand for silliness (Hosea 7:11) as well as innocence. A later midrash has God say that Israel is innocent as a dove toward him and shrewd as a serpent toward the nations (Song of Songs Rabbah 2:14). ‘Head of the house’ (oikodespotēs, verse 25) plays on Beelzebul, since zebul can mean dwelling or exalted house (1 Kings 8:13): if the master of the house is called lord of the house, so will his household be. Flat roofs served as platforms for public announcements. ‘The very hairs of your head are all numbered’ echoes the Old Testament idiom that not one hair will fall (1 Samuel 14:45).

Hell in verse 28 translates Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where kings of Judah had burned children (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 7:31); by Jesus' day its name meant the place of final judgment. The cross of verse 38 meant only one thing to first-century ears: Rome's execution for slaves and rebels, in which the condemned man carried the crossbeam to his own death. In a society where the household was the unit of work, worship, honor, and survival, a son or daughter-in-law set against the family (verses 35 and 36) faced losing home, livelihood, and name. A cup of cold water (verse 42) was the smallest act of hospitality in a dry land, and ‘little ones’ in Matthew means disciples (18:6, 18:10, 18:14).
literary:
The chapter is a speech framed by a short narrative (verses 1 to 5a) and closed in 11:1 with the formula that ends each of Matthew's five discourses. It moves in three stages. Verses 5 to 15 give practical instructions for the immediate mission. Verses 16 to 23 widen into persecution before governors and Gentiles; these sayings stand in Mark's eschatological discourse (Mark 13:9-13), and Matthew has moved them into the mission speech, keeping only a summary of them in 24:9-14, so that persecution becomes the ordinary setting of mission rather than a sign of the end. Verses 24 to 42 turn to the disciple's identity: like teacher, like disciple; fear God rather than people; loyalty to Jesus above family; and the reward for receiving his messengers. Much of this last section has parallels scattered in Luke (12:2-9, 12:51-53, 14:26-27, 17:33), which suggests that Matthew has gathered sayings on mission into one address.

Several threads bind the speech. The command ‘do not be afraid’ comes three times (verses 26, 28, 31). The word ‘worthy’ (axios) comes seven times, first of households worthy of the messengers and then of disciples worthy of Jesus (verses 37 and 38). ‘Truly I tell you’ marks three solemn sayings (verses 15, 23, 42). The verb paradidōmi, ‘hand over’, used of Judas in verse 4, returns for the disciples handed over to councils and by their own families (verses 17, 19, 21), and Matthew will use it again of Jesus' betrayal (17:22, 20:18-19, 26:2). The speech opens with authority given (verse 1) and closes with the messengers received as their sender (verse 40), an inclusion that makes the whole address a statement about who stands behind those whom Jesus sends.

outline.t: The twelve apostles named and given authority
Instructions for the mission to Israel
Do not be afraid: the Father's care and public confession
Not peace but a sword: the cost of following
Receiving the messengers and their reward

doctrines.note: The church's mission begins as a sharing in Jesus' own mission: the same message (‘the kingdom of heaven is near’, compare 4:17), the same works, the same authority, and the same dependence on God. The limit to Israel (verses 5 and 6) reflects the order of God's promises and gives way after the resurrection to the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19), while verse 18 already names the Gentiles as those before whom the disciples will testify.

Persecution is presented not as failure but as the expected lot of those who follow a rejected Master: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (verse 24). Suffering becomes testimony (verse 18), the Spirit gives words in the hour of trial (verses 19 and 20), and endurance to the end is the mark of those who are saved (verse 22).

Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father, and the hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered (verses 29 and 30). The care of God reaches to the smallest and cheapest things, which is the ground of courage in persecution rather than a promise that persecution will not come; the sparrows still fall, but not without the Father.

Jesus sets two fears side by side: the fear of those who can kill the body and the fear of the One who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna (verse 28). Rightly fearing God displaces the fear of people, and the same passage tells disciples three times not to be afraid, because the One they fear is their Father.

Verse 28 is one of the clearest statements in the Gospels that final judgment concerns the whole person, soul and body, and belongs to God alone. Christians differ on whether ‘destroy’ (apollymi) here describes unending punishment or final ruin and extinction, but agree that the verse places ultimate authority over human destiny with God, not with persecutors.

words.note: Apostolos, apostle, one who is sent. It occurs about eighty times in the New Testament, most often in Luke-Acts and Paul, but only here in Matthew. In classical Greek it could mean a naval expedition or its commander; in the New Testament it is an authorized messenger who carries the authority of the sender. The related verb apostellō, to send, appears in verses 5, 16, and 40, where ‘the One who sent Me’ shows that the chain of sending runs from the Father through Jesus to the twelve.

Axios, worthy, deserving, of fitting weight. It occurs about forty times in the New Testament, nine in Matthew, seven of them in this chapter. The worker is worthy of his food (verse 10); the messengers look for a worthy house (verses 11 and 13); and the disciple who loves family more than Jesus, or will not take up the cross, is not worthy of him (verses 37 and 38). Worthiness here is not merit earned but fitness to receive: a household is worthy by welcoming the message, a disciple by holding Jesus first.

Dechomai, to receive or welcome, especially a guest. It occurs about fifty-six times in the New Testament, ten in Matthew, seven in this chapter (verse 14, and six times in verses 40 and 41). The word joins hospitality and faith: to welcome Jesus' messengers into one's house is to welcome Jesus and the Father. The principle resembles the Jewish law of agency, summed up in the Mishnah's saying that a person's agent is like himself (m. Berakhot 5:5).

Phronimos, sensible, prudent, shrewd. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, where it describes the wise builder (7:24), the wise virgins (25:2-9), and the faithful servant (24:45). The Septuagint uses it for the serpent in Genesis 3:1. Paired with akeraios, ‘unmixed’ or ‘innocent’ (used elsewhere only in Romans 16:19 and Philippians 2:15), it asks for clear-sighted practical wisdom without guile.

Homologeō, to acknowledge or confess publicly. It occurs about twenty-six times in the New Testament, often of confessing faith (Romans 10:9, 1 John 4:2). In verses 32 and 33 it is paired with arneomai, to deny or disown, in a courtroom scene: the disciple's public loyalty before human judges is matched by Jesus' acknowledgment before the Father. Peter's denial (26:69-75) uses the same verb arneomai, and his restoration shows that the warning is not the end of the story for one who repents.

Geenna, Gehenna, the Greek form of the Hebrew gē hinnōm, the Valley of Hinnom. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, and all but one (James 3:6) on the lips of Jesus. It is distinct from Hadēs, the realm of the dead (11:23). In verse 28 it names the place where God can destroy both soul and body, the final judgment that belongs to God alone.

Machaira, sword or long knife. It occurs about twenty-nine times in the New Testament. In verse 34 it is a figure for division, as Luke's parallel makes explicit with ‘division’ (Luke 12:51); in 26:52 Jesus tells Peter to put his literal machaira away, “for all who draw the sword will die by the sword.” The sword Jesus brings is the cutting of loyalties by his claim, not a weapon for his followers to wield.

Stauros, cross, the upright stake or crossbeam of execution. It occurs about twenty-seven times in the New Testament, five in Matthew, and this is its first appearance in the Gospel, before Jesus has predicted his own death (16:21). To take up the cross was to walk toward public shame and death, and Jesus sets that as the shape of following him (compare 16:24).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the one who has authority to share his authority. He does not only heal; he empowers others to heal, cleanse, and drive out demons, and he gives them his own message. His messengers carry his presence, so that receiving them is receiving him and, through him, the Father who sent him (verse 40), a claim no prophet of Israel made for himself. He speaks as the one before whom people will be judged: whoever acknowledges him before others he will acknowledge before his Father, and whoever denies him he will deny (verses 32 and 33). Loyalty to him is set above the love of father, mother, son, and daughter (verse 37), a demand that only God could rightly make.

The warnings trace the path Jesus himself will walk. Handed over (verse 4), brought before councils and governors, flogged, and hated, the disciples will meet what Jesus meets in chapters 26 and 27, and the call to take up the cross anticipates his own. Micah 7:6, quoted in verses 35 and 36, described the breakdown of trust in a corrupt generation, and Jewish tradition read it as a sign of the days before the Messiah (m. Sotah 9:15); Jesus applies it to the division that loyalty to him will cause. The Son of Man of verse 23 is the figure of Daniel 7:13-14 who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days, and the saying about losing one's life to find it (verse 39) is the pattern of his death and resurrection laid over the lives of his followers. The mission first to the lost sheep of Israel fulfills God's promise to shepherd his scattered flock (Ezekiel 34), and after the resurrection the same Lord, with all authority, sends them to all nations (28:18-20).
interpretation:
The sayings on persecution shaped the early church's practice. Tertullian, in his Montanist period, argued in On Flight in Persecution (around 208) that verse 23 applied only to the apostles in their own time and did not license Christians to flee, while Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Cyprian treated it as permission to withdraw, and Cyprian did so during the Decian persecution of 250. Athanasius cited it in his Defence of His Flight (around 357) to justify escaping arrest, and Augustine, answering a bishop as the Vandals advanced into Africa (Letter 228, around 428), ruled that a pastor may flee if others remain to serve the people, but not if his flight would leave the flock without ministry. John Chrysostom (Homily 34 on Matthew) read verse 23 as a promise that Jesus would rejoin the twelve before they had gone through the towns, a comfort for frightened messengers.

The instructions for travel have been read literally more than once. Thomas of Celano's first Life of Francis tells how Francis of Assisi, hearing this Gospel read at the Portiuncula around 1208, took it as his rule, gave up shoes, staff, and purse, and began to preach, and the mendicant orders that followed him made evangelical poverty a way of life. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937), written while he trained pastors for the Confessing Church under Nazi rule, devotes its chapter ‘The Messengers’ to this discourse and reads its warnings of hatred and division as the normal condition of those who carry Christ's word.

Modern scholarship has argued about verse 23 more than any other verse in the chapter. Albert Schweitzer, in The Mystery of the Kingdom of God (1901) and The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906), made it the key to his reconstruction: Jesus expected the Son of Man to appear before the twelve returned, and when he did not, Jesus resolved to bring on the end through his own death. The limitation to Israel in verses 5 and 6 has also drawn attention. Joachim Jeremias (Jesus' Promise to the Nations, English 1958) argued that Jesus limited his own mission to Israel while expecting the nations to stream in at the end, as the prophets foresaw. Amy-Jill Levine (The Social and Ethnic Dimensions of Matthean Salvation History, 1988) challenged readings that dismissed the saying as the relic of a narrow Jewish-Christian source, and read Matthew as moving in stages from Israel to the nations without rejecting Israel. David Sim (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 1995) argued that Matthew's community, though it accepted a Gentile mission in principle, did not take part in one.

Jewish readers have recognized the Micah saying of verses 35 and 36; the Mishnah uses the same verse to describe the disorders of the days before the Messiah (m. Sotah 9:15). The chapter is read in the Revised Common Lectionary on three consecutive Sundays in June of Year A (9:35-10:23, 10:24-39, 10:40-42), and it is a traditional reading on the feasts of apostles, whose calling and sending it records.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points. In verse 3 the earliest manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read Thaddaeus; Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies read Lebbaeus; and the later manuscripts behind the King James Version combine them as ‘Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus’. In verse 4 the King James Version renders Kananaios as ‘the Canaanite’, as if it named a place; it comes from the Aramaic for zealous, and modern versions read ‘the Zealot’ or ‘the Cananaean’.

In verse 8 the words ‘raise the dead’ are in the early manuscripts and the Textus Receptus behind the King James Version, but are missing from most later Byzantine manuscripts, probably because a copyist's eye skipped among the five commands ending in the same letters. In verse 23 Codex Bezae and some other witnesses add ‘and if they persecute you in the other, flee to another’. In verse 6 the Greek says ‘the lost sheep of the house of Israel’, as in 15:24; the BSB shortens it to ‘the lost sheep of Israel’. In verse 29 the Greek says only that no sparrow falls ‘without your Father’; ‘the will of’ is supplied by the BSB and many other versions, while others keep the bare phrase, which speaks of the Father's presence and knowledge as much as his decree. The King James Version's ‘farthing’ for the assarion was an English coin worth a quarter of a penny.

teach.big: Jesus sends his disciples with his own authority and message into a world that will treat them as it treated him, frees them from fear by the Father's care, and binds them to himself above every other loyalty.

outline.t: Jesus shares his authority with ordinary, named people, from a fisherman to a tax collector, a zealot, and a betrayer.
The message and the mercy go together: announce the kingdom and do its works, giving freely what was freely received.
Messengers depend on God and on those who welcome them, and the response to the message carries eternal weight.
Mission happens among wolves, so disciples need shrewdness without guile, trust in the Spirit's help, and endurance to the end.
A disciple should expect the treatment his Teacher received; the insult to the Master falls on his household.
Fear of people is driven out by the fear of God and by the Father's care for sparrows and for every hair.
Public loyalty to Jesus before people is answered by his loyalty to us before the Father.
Jesus' claim can divide even families, because he must be loved above all; the life surrendered for him is the life found.
To receive Christ's messengers is to receive Christ and the Father, and even a cup of cold water given for his sake is not forgotten.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats verses 5 and 6 either as proof that Jesus despised Gentiles or as a sign that God has finished with Israel; the limit is a matter of order in God's plan, Matthew's Gospel has already honored Gentiles (1:3-6, 2:1-12, 8:5-13) and will end with the nations (28:19), and Jesus goes to Israel first because of God's faithfulness to Israel. The second turns verses 9 and 10 into a fixed rule for every minister, or the opposite, a text for raising funds; the command fits a short, urgent mission in Galilean villages, and the principle is dependence and generosity, not a single economic model. The third reads verse 34 as permission for religious violence or for a combative spirit; the sword is the division that comes when people respond differently to Jesus, and Jesus rebukes the literal sword in 26:52. The fourth uses verses 35 to 37 to excuse neglect of family, which Jesus condemns in 15:3-6.

Two further errors concern fear and suffering. Verse 28 has been used to frighten people into belief, but the passage uses the fear of God to free disciples from the fear of people and in the same breath tells them three times not to be afraid. Verses 29 to 31 are sometimes preached as fatalism, as if God sends every harm; the point is that nothing falls outside the Father's knowledge and care. And the warnings of persecution should not be applied to every inconvenience or criticism a comfortable church meets; they describe courts, floggings, and death, which many Christians in the world still face.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will reach people whose faith has cost them family: converts disowned by parents, spouses of different faith, young people whose calling was mocked at home. Teach verses 34 to 37 as Jesus' acknowledgment of their pain, not as a command to break relationships; he asks for first loyalty, not for coldness, and the new family of 12:49-50 is meant to receive them. The same verses must never be used to keep someone in an abusive home in the name of carrying a cross, or to tell victims that their suffering is God's will for them; the cross is taken up for Christ's sake, not handed out by abusers. Those who have lost loved ones to violence or persecution may hear ‘not one of them will fall’ as either comfort or accusation, so say plainly that the sparrows do fall, and that the Father is present in their falling. For those gripped by fear of death, verse 28 is meant as release: those who can kill the body cannot touch the soul.

hard.q: Why does Jesus forbid the twelve to go to Gentiles and Samaritans, when he later sends them to all nations?
hard.a:
The objection comes from several directions. Critical scholars have often taken verses 5 and 6, with 15:24, as evidence that the historical Jesus confined his mission to Israel and that the Gentile mission was the church's later development, read back into the Gospel in 28:19; on this view Matthew preserves two incompatible layers. David Sim (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 1995) argued that the Gospel's outlook is not only Jewish but anti-Gentile, and that its community did not itself pursue a Gentile mission. Others, Christian and Jewish, have been troubled by the ethnic limit itself: it can sound as though God's kindness stops at a border. And Christian readers have sometimes used the verse the opposite way, as proof that Israel's time is over once the church turns to the nations, a reading Jewish scholars have rightly resisted.

The main responses read the limit as a matter of sequence. Paul describes the same order: the gospel is ‘to the Jew first, and also to the Greek’ (Romans 1:16), and in Acts the apostles turn to the Gentiles after preaching first in the synagogues (Acts 13:46). Joachim Jeremias (Jesus' Promise to the Nations, 1958) argued that Jesus limited his earthly mission to Israel while expecting the nations to come in at the end, as Isaiah foresaw, so that 28:19 fulfills rather than contradicts the first mission. Amy-Jill Levine (1988) argued that Matthew traces a salvation history in which the mission moves from Israel to the nations without Israel being excluded, since 28:19's ‘all nations’ includes Israel. Many commentators add that Matthew's own Gospel has already honored Gentiles, from the women of the genealogy and the Magi to the centurion, and that verse 18 in this very chapter sends the disciples before Gentiles as witnesses. Readers differ on how much of this reflects the historical Jesus and how much Matthew's arrangement, but the chapter itself frames the limit as a first step in a mission that will reach the ends of the earth.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean by “you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes”?
hard.a:
Verse 23 seems to set a time limit on the coming of the Son of Man, and the strongest objection is that it failed. Albert Schweitzer, in The Mystery of the Kingdom of God (1901) and The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906), built his portrait of Jesus on this verse: Jesus expected the end to come while the twelve were still on the road, and when they returned and nothing had happened, he resolved to force the end by going to his death. Skeptical readers have taken the verse as one of several unfulfilled predictions of an imminent end (compare 16:28, 24:34), and some Christians have felt the difficulty keenly.

The main responses take different views of what ‘comes’ means. John Chrysostom (Homily 34 on Matthew) read it as a promise that Jesus would rejoin the twelve during this very mission, before they had covered the towns. Tertullian (On Flight in Persecution) limited it to the apostles' own time and circumstances. Many interpreters connect it with Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive dominion, and so read it of Jesus' vindication: some place that at his resurrection, when he announces that all authority has been given to him (28:18), and R. T. France (The Gospel of Matthew, 2007) sees the vindication made visible in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which chapter 24 links with the Son of Man's coming. W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, in their commentary on Matthew, and Ulrich Luz read it of the final coming and note that Matthew never says the mission to Israel was completed; it continues until the Son of Man returns, so the saying describes an unfinished task rather than a missed date. Each view has careful defenders, and the chapter's own widening scope, reaching beyond the first mission to governors and Gentiles, is part of what makes the verse hard to pin down. What all agree on is its purpose in context: persecuted messengers are to keep moving, because their Lord's coming will overtake their work, not the other way round.

observe: What authority does Jesus give the twelve in verse 1, and how do the works he lists in verse 8 match what he himself has done in chapters 8 and 9?
How many times does Jesus say ‘do not be afraid’ in verses 26 to 31, and what reason does he give each time?
Which kinds of people are named as receiving Jesus' messengers in verses 40 to 42, and what is promised to them?
interpret: Why does Jesus limit this first mission to the lost sheep of Israel, and how does that limit relate to 10:18 and 28:19?
How can the same passage tell disciples to fear God (verse 28) and not to be afraid (verses 26 and 31)?
In what sense does Jesus bring ‘not peace but a sword’, and how does that fit with his blessing on peacemakers (5:9)?
apply: Where are you most tempted to hide your loyalty to Jesus, and what would it mean to acknowledge him there?
Is there a relationship in your life where following Jesus has caused tension? How can you keep him first and still love that person well?
Who are the ‘little ones’ near you who need a cup of cold water, and what small act of welcome could you offer this week?
